title: What Changed After Sixty
paragraphs: I asked one of my friends who had turned sixty and was nearing seventy what change he felt in himself. This was his answer:
I stopped telling older people, “You’ve told that story before.” After all, those conversations help them revive dear memories and live those beautiful moments again.
I learned not to correct people even when they are wrong. After all, making everyone perfect is not my job. Peace matters more than perfection.
I offer compliments freely. After all, it pleases not only the person before me, but my own soul as well.
I learned not to fret over a crease or a stain on my clothes. In the end, a person’s worth comes not from outward appearance, but from within.
I learned to keep my distance from people who are strangers to my world. After all, they cannot build and keep a good relationship—and I have learned that too.
I learned not to be ashamed of my feelings. After all, it is my feelings that make me human.
I learned that setting ego aside is better than breaking relationships. After all, ego leads me to loneliness, while relationships help me not to be alone.
I learned to do the things that can make me happy. After all, I myself am responsible for my own happiness.
I learned not to help when it is not wanted. After all, someone who needs help may not want that help to come from me.

I learned not to complain about my health, my neighbors, my relatives, or being a pensioner! After all, despite every difficulty, I ought to give thanks that I am alive and that my loved ones are beside me.

I gave up saying things to the young like “When I was your age…”; and I never use phrases like “I gave you my best years…” After all, every time has its own judgment, and it is not right to apply the standards of the past to the present.

Without forgetting that he was once young, strong, and full of joy, I began to pay more attention to my spouse—even if he is now a wrinkled, helpless, and sorrowful old man. After all, he may be the only person who truly needs me in this moment.
I stopped blaming myself for everything. After all, in life I have done all I could for myself and for my children.
And finally: I learned to ask my Lord for strength for what I can change, patience for what I cannot, and wisdom to tell the two apart. After all, as a human being I am not all-powerful.
Age teaches a person the greatest wisdom: peace is better than perfection, and understanding is better than being proved right.

title: For Those Who Have Reached Sixty…
paragraphs: It is time to use the money you have saved until today. Use it and enjoy it. Do not save it for those who know nothing of the sacrifices you made to earn it. This is the ideal time to savor peace.

Do not worry about the finances of your children and grandchildren, and do not feel guilty for spending your money on yourself. For years you cared for them and taught them everything you could. You gave them education, food, shelter, and support. Now it is their duty to earn their own money. Let them find their own way.
Now live a healthy life without exhausting too much physical strength. Exercise moderately, take a walk every day, eat well, and sleep well.

At this age it is easy to fall ill and hard to stay healthy. That is why you must keep yourself in good condition and attend to your medical and physical needs. Stay in touch with your doctor; even if you feel well, go for checkups.

Do not stress over small things. You have already overcome so much in life. You have good memories and bad ones. Do not let the past pull you back or the future frighten you. Feel good now. Small troubles will soon be forgotten.
Whatever your age, keep living your love. Love your spouse, love life, love your family—and remember: so long as your mind and your kindness are intact, you are not old.

Do not stop going to the barber; care for your nails; see a dermatologist and a dentist; use perfume and creams. When you look well cared for on the outside, that feeling seeps inward too, and you will feel proud and strong.

Do not overlook age-appropriate fashion trends, but keep your own style. Read books, glance through the newspapers, watch the news. Go online and learn what people are thinking. Make sure you have an active email account and use at least a few social networks.

Respect the younger generation and their views. They may not agree with you, yet the future is theirs, and they will steer their lives as they wish. Do not criticize; offer counsel, and try to remind them that yesterday’s wisdom can still hold true today.
Never use the phrase “In our day…” This is your time now. As long as you live, be a part of this age.
Try to stay away from negative people and spend your time with those who give you only good spirits and positive energy.
Do not give up your hobbies. You can travel, walk, cook, read, dance. If you wish, you can keep a cat or a dog.
Leave the house; meet people you have not seen in a long time; live something new or something old again. What matters is that you step outside from time to time. Visit museums; walk in the park.
Always try to be courteous, and do not complain or criticize unless necessary. If someone has broken your heart, forgive them. And ask forgiveness of those whose hearts you have broken.

Do not carry your bitterness with you. It only hurts you. It does not matter who was right. They say holding a grudge is like poisoning yourself and waiting for the other person to die. Never take that poison. Forgive, forget, and go on with your life.
Laugh, rejoice. In this season of your life, savor a peaceful existence… Be happy!
The time of sacrifice one day comes to an end; in the autumn of life, grant yourself the right to live as well. A happy person spreads happiness to those around them.

title: Aging
paragraphs: Growing old is like climbing a mountain: the higher you go, the more tired you grow and the shorter your breath becomes—but your view of the world widens.
Growing old is like climbing a mountain: your breath grows short, but your view of the world widens. The increase of years is also the increase of wisdom.

title: Albrecht Dürer
paragraphs: In a small village near Nuremberg lived a family with ten children. To provide for them, the father had to work eighteen hours a day. Despite that desperate hardship, the two eldest sons—Albrecht and Albert—dreamed of becoming renowned artists. Yet they knew their father could not afford to educate both of them at once.

After long discussions by candlelight, the brothers decided to draw lots. The terms were simple: the winner would go to the academy in Nuremberg, and the loser would work in a nearby mine to support him. After four years they would switch places.
Albrecht Dürer won the lot. As agreed, he set off for the academy, and Albert began work in the mine.

Over the next four years one brother devoted himself to painting while the other labored in the depths of the mine. Albrecht’s works soon aroused great interest; it was said that his art was stronger even than that of most of his teachers.
When he finished his studies, Albrecht was already earning enough. After the four years were over, he returned home with joy and said to his brother:
— Dear brother, now it is your turn. Go and make your dreams come true; this time I will support you.
But Albert’s wish was not to be fulfilled. Holding out his hands to his brother, he said quietly:
— No, my brother. I can no longer go to Nuremberg; it is too late. See how in these four years the mine has crushed my hands, every finger. I can no longer paint.
Albrecht took his beloved brother’s hands in his palms and was overcome with tears.

Though centuries have passed, the works of Albrecht Dürer (21.05.1471 – 06.04.1528) are still displayed today in the world’s most prestigious art galleries. The famous work he dedicated to his brother is known worldwide as “Praying Hands” and is now kept in the Albertina gallery in Vienna.
Behind every success stands an unseen sacrifice. To see that sacrifice and value it is one of the finest signs of humanity.

title: Architect Sinan, Who Brought Water to Istanbul, Dies in a House Without Water
paragraphs: It is the reign of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. Istanbul, whose population grows by the day, suffers from a shortage of water. The easing of that shortage is bound up with the name of one of the eminent figures of the age, the elder Master Architect Sinan Aga (1489–1588; he lived ninety-nine years).

One day Sultan Suleiman summoned Architect Sinan and said: “Chief Architect, the people need water. Folk pay a great deal of coin for a single horse-load of water. Might you think of a way to meet this need?” The Chief Architect replied: “My Sultan, grant me leave to tour the surroundings of Istanbul, to see whether the existing waters can be brought into the city, and then I will give you my answer.”

Sinan Aga took his assistants and, beginning from Chekmeca, went from well to well, identifying the valleys and flowing streams as far as Besiktas. If dams were built upon these waters, how high would they rise, and from where to where might aqueducts be laid to bring them into Istanbul—after studying such questions and making his calculations, he again appeared before the Sultan.

The Sultan asked: “Chief Architect, is it possible to bring water to Istanbul?” “Yes, my Sultan, it is possible. But there is a very heavy condition.” “What is it, Chief Architect?” “My Sultan, water can come to Istanbul only on the condition that sacks filled with gold be stacked end to end.” “Chief Architect, only tell me that bringing water to Istanbul is possible! If the work can be done, I am ready to stack the sacks not merely end to end, but side by side as well.”

Architect Sinan rolled up his sleeves and set to work, and completed this magnificent project that ended with forty fountains being built in Istanbul’s known squares. Through those forty fountains Istanbul was joined to water. To keep the water from running to waste, taps (faucets) were fitted to the fountains.

Because the water had cost so much and risen so high in value, the Sultan issued a decree: “The public fountains in Istanbul’s squares are the property of the people; no one may secretly draw water underground into his own house.” Even so, Sultan Suleiman added an exception to that decree for Architect Sinan: “You have done a fine work and brought forty fountains to Istanbul. Now you may draw water into your own house for yourself.” A private water pipe was laid from the square fountain near the Suleymaniye to Sinan’s house. Thus Architect Sinan became the only person in the whole city with private water in his home.

After building the mosques of Sehzadebasi, the Suleymaniye, and the Selimiye in Edirne, Architect Sinan grew old. Those who had known his worth in the days when his standing was high had already departed this world one by one. Sultan Suleiman had died, and other sultans had taken his place. Sinan himself had reached ninety-nine, and with his friends gone he was left alone in Istanbul.

One day someone came and knocked at Sinan’s door: “I am from Topkapi Palace; they summon you to the council,” he said. At that advanced age Sinan Aga set out for the palace, wondering, “Why might they be calling me to Topkapi?”

When he arrived he saw that an inquiry panel had gathered—judges, scholars, muftis, and viziers. They said to Sinan: “Sinan Aga, there is a complaint against you. Though drawing water into a private house is forbidden, and though there is a royal decree that no one may bring private water into his home, it seems there is private water in your house.”
Sinan replied: “At that time the Padishah of the World, for the water services I rendered to Istanbul, gave leave for water in my house to me alone.”
“Then show us that leave, that decree, so that we may hold our peace and your water may keep flowing, even though it was granted to no one else.”
Sinan said: “In those days I was ashamed to ask the Padishah of the World for a decree. I have no decree or the like—but I do have water in my house.”

The council found itself in a difficult position; all sorts of opinions were voiced: “Sinan has rendered great services; let him keep water in his house.” Others answered: “Has only Sinan served this state? There are many who have served as Sinan has. Either let private water be given to their houses too, or let this privilege granted to Sinan not be recognized.”

After long debate the council ruled: “Because water will not be brought into the houses of others who have rendered great services like Sinan’s, the water given to Sinan must be cut off; yet he is to suffer no punishment for the water he has used until now without a decree in hand.”
They cut off Sinan’s water.

When the architect reached the age of one hundred he fell ill and took to his bed. As he was dying, those around him asked for water to wet his lips and saw that none came from the tap in his house. Seeing this, Sinan said to them: “We did not serve for gain. We did it for God, and we shall await our reward in the hereafter. We do not grieve that in this world water was not given to our house.”
Do not put too much trust in the world, in fame, or in the loyalty of people. True service is done not for profit, but for the Truth.
